did_you_know.text: Did you know? The confrontation between Jeremiah and Hananiah took place in the temple, in the fourth year of Zedekiah’s reign and in the fifth month, in the presence of the priests and all the people.
Did you know? Hananiah son of Azzur is described as a prophet from Gibeon, and he proclaimed his message publicly in the name of the LORD.
Did you know? Hananiah set a clear, short timetable: within two years, the vessels of the temple that had been taken to Babylon would be returned.
Did you know? Hananiah’s prophecy included not only the return of the temple vessels, but also the return of Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim and all the exiles of Judah from Babylon.

Did you know? Jeremiah replied to Hananiah, “Amen! May the LORD do so,” expressing hope that the prophecy of peace and restoration would indeed come true, though he did not confirm that it was a true prophecy.
Did you know? Jeremiah presented a test for a prophet who proclaims peace: the truth of the prophecy will be known when the prophet’s word comes to pass.
Did you know? Hananiah illustrated his prophecy with a symbolic act: he took the yoke from Jeremiah’s neck and broke it in the presence of the people.
Did you know? After the wooden yokes were broken, Jeremiah was instructed to announce that they would be replaced with iron yokes, symbolizing a stronger and harsher oppression upon the nations.
Did you know? Jeremiah stated explicitly that Hananiah had not been sent by the LORD and that, by making this promise to the people, he had caused them to trust in a lie.
Did you know? According to the end of the chapter, Hananiah died that same year in which the prophecy concerning him was given, in the seventh month.
